title: How the Body Stays Alive
summary: The one job every body has: get oxygen and glucose to cells and haul carbon dioxide away. Everything else in medicine is a story about that delivery failing.

lessons.title: The whole game: oxygen in, CO2 out
lessons.body:
## The whole game in one sentence

Your body is roughly 30 trillion cells, and every one of them is a tiny engine. Each engine burns sugar (`glucose`) using oxygen (`O2`) to make the only fuel a cell can actually spend, a molecule called `ATP`.

The reaction is simple to say: glucose plus oxygen goes in, `ATP` comes out, and carbon dioxide (`CO2`) plus water come out as exhaust. That is it. Everything you will learn about airway, breathing, circulation, and shock is a story about keeping that reaction running.

> **Key:** Deliver oxygen and glucose to cells, carry `CO2` away. Every emergency is a failure somewhere in that delivery chain.

## Why oxygen matters so much

With oxygen, one glucose molecule yields about `30` to `32 ATP`. That is aerobic metabolism, and aerobic just means with air.

Without oxygen, the cell can still split glucose, but it gets only `2 ATP` from it, and it dumps lactic acid as a byproduct. That is anaerobic metabolism.

So a cell without oxygen is not simply working slower. It is running at roughly six percent power while acidifying its own neighborhood. That acid is why a patient in shock develops a low blood pH (metabolic acidosis) long before anything looks dramatic.

## Why glucose matters just as much

Most cells can burn fat or protein when sugar runs short. Brain cells largely cannot. They run on glucose almost exclusively and store almost none.

That is why a blood sugar under `70 mg/dL` can make a person confused, combative, or unconscious within minutes, and why a diabetic patient with a sugar of `40 mg/dL` can look exactly like a stroke. Give sugar and the stroke walks away. This is the most reversible cause of altered mental status you will ever meet.

> **On shift:** Any patient with altered mental status gets a fingerstick glucose. Not eventually. Early, every time.

## Why CO2 has to leave

Carbon dioxide is not just waste taking up space. When `CO2` dissolves in blood it forms carbonic acid. Hold `CO2` in and blood pH falls. Blow `CO2` off and pH rises.

That is why a patient who stops breathing adequately becomes acidotic within minutes, and why a panicking patient breathing `40` times a minute gets tingling hands and lips. They have blown their `CO2` too low and the blood has turned alkaline.

## The clock

Different tissues tolerate no oxygen for very different lengths of time.

| Tissue | Rough tolerance without oxygen |
|---|---|
| Brain | `4`–`6` minutes before damage begins |
| Heart muscle | `20`–`30` minutes |
| Kidney | `30`–`60` minutes |
| Skeletal muscle | `2`–`4` hours |
| Skin and bone | many hours |

The brain's `4`–`6` minute window is the reason CPR exists, the reason airway comes first, and the reason nobody in this field is casual about a pulse check.

> **On the exam:** When one answer restores oxygen delivery and another gathers more information, oxygen delivery wins.
keyPoints: Cells burn glucose with oxygen to make ATP; CO2 and water are the exhaust.
Aerobic metabolism gives about 30–32 ATP per glucose; anaerobic gives 2 plus lactic acid.
The brain runs on glucose and stores almost none, so check a sugar on every altered patient.
Retained CO2 acidifies blood; blown-off CO2 makes it alkaline.
Brain damage begins at 4–6 minutes without oxygen.

checks.q: A cell is cut off from oxygen but still has plenty of glucose. What happens?
choices: It makes the same ATP by a different route
It makes about 2 ATP per glucose and produces lactic acid
It stops all metabolism instantly
It switches to burning CO2 for fuel
checks.why: Anaerobic metabolism still splits glucose but yields only 2 ATP instead of 30–32, and the leftover is lactic acid. The cell is not dead, it is starved and acidifying.

checks.q: Why does a blood glucose of 45 mg/dL cause confusion within minutes?
choices: Low sugar thickens the blood and slows flow
Brain cells run almost entirely on glucose and store almost none
Low sugar makes the airway swell
Glucose is what carries oxygen in the blood
checks.why: The brain has no meaningful glucose reserve and cannot readily burn fat, so supply interruption shows up as mental status change almost immediately. Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin, not glucose.

checks.q: A panicking patient breathes 40 times a minute and reports tingling lips and fingers. What changed?
choices: CO2 has been blown off and the blood has turned alkaline
Oxygen has reached a toxic level
The breathing muscles used up the available glucose
CO2 has built up and the blood has turned acidic
checks.why: Fast breathing removes CO2, and less CO2 means less carbonic acid, so pH rises into alkalosis. Tingling around the mouth and in the fingers is the classic sign. Oxygen toxicity does not occur from room air breathing.

lessons.title: Perfusion: pump, pipes, fluid, air
lessons.body:
## Delivery is a plumbing problem

Cells need oxygen and glucose delivered and `CO2` hauled away. The delivery service is blood, and the act of delivering is called **perfusion**: blood actually reaching tissue and exchanging with it.

Perfusion needs four things working at the same time. Lose any one and delivery fails.

1. A **pump** — the heart, moving about `5 L` of blood every minute at rest
2. **Pipes** — arteries, arterioles, capillaries and veins, sized correctly
3. **Fluid** — enough blood volume to fill those pipes, roughly `5 L` in an average adult
4. **Air** — lungs loading oxygen onto blood and unloading `CO2`

> **Key:** Pump, pipes, fluid, air. Every family of shock you will ever learn is one of those four failing.

## The pump

Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate. Stroke volume is how much blood leaves the left ventricle per beat, normally `60`–`100 mL`. Heart rate is beats per minute.

`70 mL × 70 beats/min` is about `4,900 mL/min`, so roughly `5 L` per minute. The body's entire blood volume circulates about once a minute at rest.

Notice what that equation permits. If stroke volume falls, the body can hold cardiac output steady by raising rate. That single fact explains most of the vital sign patterns in this course.

## The pipes

Blood pressure is not just the pump pushing. It is the pump pushing against resistance, and resistance is set almost entirely by the diameter of the small arteries (arterioles).

Narrowing them raises pressure and shunts blood toward the core. Widening them (vasodilation) drops pressure quickly, because the same `5 L` now has to fill a much larger container.

> **Trap:** A patient can have every drop of their blood and still be in shock if the pipes are too wide. Nothing was lost; the container got bigger.

## The fluid

An adult holds about `5 L`, roughly `70 mL/kg`. Losing about `15%` (around `750 mL`) is usually tolerated with almost no change in blood pressure. Losing `30%`–`40%`, meaning `1.5`–`2 L`, drops pressure and is immediately life-threatening.

Fluid can be lost outward through bleeding, vomiting, diarrhea, or burns. It can also leak inward into tissue, where it is still inside the body but no longer circulating. Both count as volume loss.

## The air

Perfusion delivers whatever the blood happens to be carrying. If the lungs never loaded oxygen, perfect circulation is just empty trucks running on time.

This is why two words get separated constantly in this field. **Oxygenation** is getting oxygen into blood. **Ventilation** is moving air in and out to clear `CO2`. A patient can fail at either one alone, and the fix is different.

## Reading perfusion at the bedside

You cannot see cardiac output. You can see its shadow.

- Skin color, temperature and moisture — cool, pale, clammy means arterioles have clamped down
- Capillary refill — press a nail bed and release; color should return in under `2` seconds
- Mental status — the brain complains first
- Urine output — `0.5 mL/kg/hr` in an adult is the floor
- Pulse quality — weak and thready means low stroke volume

> **On shift:** Pale, cool, clammy skin with a fast pulse is a perfusion problem until proven otherwise, no matter what the blood pressure reads.
keyPoints: Perfusion needs pump, pipes, fluid and air all at once.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate; about 70 mL × 70 bpm ≈ 5 L/min.
Blood pressure is cardiac output times vessel resistance, so dilated pipes drop pressure with no blood lost.
An adult tolerates about 15% volume loss; 30–40% loss drops pressure.
Skin signs, capillary refill under 2 seconds, mental status and pulse quality are your bedside perfusion meters.

checks.q: A patient's stroke volume falls from 70 mL to 50 mL. How does the body keep cardiac output near normal?
choices: By raising the heart rate
By lowering the heart rate to allow more filling
By increasing the respiratory rate
By raising body temperature
checks.why: Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate, so a smaller stroke volume is offset by more beats per minute. That is why tachycardia is the earliest cardiovascular sign of trouble.

checks.q: Which finding most directly tells you the arterioles have constricted?
choices: A respiratory rate of 22
A blood pressure of 118/76
Pale, cool, clammy skin
A temperature of 37.2 C
checks.why: Blood is being pulled out of the skin to protect the core, which makes skin pale and cool, and the same sympathetic surge turns on sweat glands. A normal blood pressure does not rule this out; it often means compensation is still working.

checks.q: What is the difference between oxygenation and ventilation?
choices: They are two words for the same process
Oxygenation is getting oxygen into blood; ventilation is moving air to clear CO2
Oxygenation happens in the heart; ventilation happens in the lungs
Ventilation refers only to mechanical ventilators
checks.why: They are separate jobs and can fail separately. A patient can have a normal SpO2 on oxygen while retaining dangerous amounts of CO2 because they are not moving enough air.

lessons.title: What kills you first: A, B, C, then the brain
lessons.body:
## Why the order is the order

You will hear airway, breathing, circulation a thousand times. It is not tradition. It is a ranking by how fast each failure kills.

| Failure | Time to death or permanent damage |
|---|---|
| Blocked airway | `4`–`6` minutes |
| Not breathing | `4`–`6` minutes |
| No circulation | `4`–`6` minutes to brain damage |
| Massive bleeding | `3` minutes to hours, depending on the vessel |
| Brain injury and most everything else | hours |

The three fast failures all end in the same place: a brain out of oxygen in `4`–`6` minutes. You fix them in an order set by dependency, because each step is useless without the one before it.

> **Key:** A perfect airway does nothing if the patient is not breathing. Perfect breathing does nothing if blood is not moving. The order is a chain, not a preference.

## A — Airway

The airway is the pipe from mouth and nose down to the lungs. Blocked, nothing you do reaches a single cell.

In an unconscious adult lying face up, the most common blockage is the tongue falling back against the throat, because the muscle tone holding it forward is gone. That is why a head-tilt chin-lift, or a jaw-thrust when spine injury is suspected, fixes so many patients who looked like they had stopped breathing.

Other blockers: vomit, blood, broken teeth, food, and swelling from burns or allergic reaction.

## B — Breathing

An open airway does not guarantee air is moving. Breathing means an adequate rate **and** an adequate depth (tidal volume).

An adult breathing `8` times a minute is moving about half the air of one breathing `16`. An adult breathing `40` shallow breaths a minute may be moving almost nothing useful, because each tiny breath mostly refills the roughly `150 mL` of anatomic dead space in the trachea and bronchi and never reaches the alveoli.

> **Trap:** Rate alone never tells you whether breathing is adequate. Fast and shallow is as dangerous as slow.

## C — Circulation

Circulation is blood actually moving. You assess it with pulse, skin signs, and a search for bleeding.

Massive external bleeding is the one finding that legitimately jumps the line. Current trauma practice stops catastrophic hemorrhage first and then returns to the airway, because a torn femoral artery can empty an adult in under `3` minutes and no airway maneuver will outrun that.

## D — Disability, meaning the brain

Once air and blood are moving, check the organ they were protecting: level of consciousness, pupils, movement and sensation in all four limbs, and blood glucose.

The brain is last in the sequence because you cannot fix it without the first three, not because it matters least. It is the reason for all of it.

## E — Exposure

Finally you look at the whole patient, front and back, because you cannot treat an injury you never uncovered. Then cover them again; a cold patient clots poorly and bleeds more.

> **On the exam:** When a question hands you several abnormal findings at once, act in ABC order. The credited answer is almost always the one highest in the alphabet.
keyPoints: The ABC order ranks failures by speed of death, and each step depends on the one before it.
In an unconscious adult the tongue is the most common airway obstruction; head-tilt chin-lift or jaw-thrust fixes it.
Breathing needs adequate rate and adequate depth; about 150 mL of each breath is dead space.
Catastrophic external bleeding is the only finding that comes before airway.
Disability (brain) and exposure come after air and blood are moving.

checks.q: An unconscious adult lying face up has snoring respirations. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Fluid in the alveoli
The tongue falling back against the throat
A collapsed lung
Low blood glucose
checks.why: Loss of muscle tone lets the tongue fall back and partially obstruct the airway, which produces snoring. It is corrected by a head-tilt chin-lift or a jaw-thrust, not by giving oxygen through a blocked pipe.

checks.q: Which patient is moving the least useful air?
choices: Adult at 16 breaths per minute, normal depth
Adult at 12 breaths per minute, normal depth
Adult at 20 breaths per minute, normal depth
Adult at 40 breaths per minute, very shallow
checks.why: Each very shallow breath mostly refills the roughly 150 mL of dead space and barely reaches the alveoli, so gas exchange collapses even though the rate looks alarmingly high. Rate without depth is meaningless.

checks.q: A trauma patient has spurting blood from a thigh wound and noisy breathing. What comes first?
choices: Control the catastrophic bleeding, then address the airway
Open the airway first, then look for bleeding
Take a full set of vital signs first
Check pupils and glucose first
checks.why: Massive external hemorrhage is the one exception that precedes the airway, because an arterial bleed can empty an adult in under 3 minutes. Everything else still follows airway, breathing, circulation.

lessons.title: Homeostasis and compensation: why the pulse moves first
lessons.body:
## The body defends set points

Homeostasis means staying the same. The body works constantly to hold temperature, pH, blood sugar, oxygen and blood pressure inside narrow bands.

Every regulated value uses the same machinery: a sensor detects drift, a control center compares it to the set point, and an effector pushes back. Temperature drifts down, you shiver. Blood sugar rises, you release insulin.

> **Key:** Vital signs are not the disease. They are the body's answer to the disease. Read them as responses, not as the problem itself.

## The pressure defense

Blood pressure is guarded by stretch sensors called baroreceptors in the carotid arteries and the aortic arch. When pressure falls, stretch falls, and the sympathetic nervous system fires.

It makes three moves:

1. Raises heart rate — more beats per minute
2. Raises contractility — each squeeze is harder
3. Narrows arterioles in skin, gut and muscle — vasoconstriction

Hold those next to the two equations from the last lesson. Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate. Blood pressure is cardiac output times resistance. If stroke volume drops because volume was lost, raising rate keeps output steady, and narrowing pipes keeps pressure steady.

So the pulse rises **before** the pressure falls. A falling blood pressure does not mean shock is starting. It means compensation has already failed.

## Why the skin goes pale, cool and clammy

Vasoconstriction is selective. The body sacrifices skin, gut and muscle to protect brain, heart and kidneys.

- Less blood in skin means pale color and cool temperature
- The same sympathetic surge fires sweat glands, so the skin is also wet
- Together: pale, cool, diaphoretic, which is the classic shock skin

Skin is the earliest window you have and it costs nothing to look at.

## Compensated versus decompensated

**Compensated shock** means perfusion is already inadequate but the defenses are holding the numbers up. Expect a fast pulse, fast breathing, an anxious or restless patient, pale cool skin, delayed capillary refill, and a narrowing pulse pressure, all with a normal or near-normal blood pressure.

**Decompensated shock** means the defenses have failed. Blood pressure falls, mental status drops, the pulse becomes weak and may eventually slow. This is late, and the patient is close to arrest.

Pulse pressure deserves its own line. It is systolic minus diastolic, normally about `30`–`40 mmHg`. In early hypovolemic shock the diastolic rises toward the systolic as vessels clamp, so `120/80` becomes `118/96`. The systolic looks untouched and the patient is in trouble.

> **Trap:** The blood pressure was normal is not reassurance. In an adult, pressure commonly holds until roughly `30%` of blood volume is gone.

## Why children fool you, then crash

Children compensate better than adults. A child can raise heart rate enormously and clamp vessels hard, so a child may lose `30%`–`40%` of blood volume with a blood pressure that still reads normal for age.

Then the reserve runs out all at once, and the fall is steep. Pediatric hypotension is a pre-arrest finding, not an early warning. In a child, judge perfusion by heart rate, skin, capillary refill, and alertness, and treat on those.

A useful floor for the lowest acceptable systolic in a child aged `1`–`10` is `70 + (2 × age in years)`. Below that, act immediately.

> **On shift:** A quiet, floppy child who was screaming ten minutes ago has not calmed down. That is a brain losing perfusion.
keyPoints: Compensation raises heart rate, contractility and vessel tone to defend blood pressure.
Heart rate rises before blood pressure falls; hypotension means compensation already failed.
Pale, cool, clammy skin is selective vasoconstriction plus sympathetic sweating.
Normal pulse pressure is 30–40 mmHg; narrowing pulse pressure is an early hypovolemia clue.
Children hold pressure until 30–40% volume loss, then crash; minimum systolic is 70 + (2 × age).

checks.q: An adult trauma patient has HR 124, BP 118/96, cool pale skin and capillary refill of 4 seconds. How do you classify this?
choices: Not in shock, since the blood pressure is normal
Compensated shock
Decompensated shock
Neurogenic shock
checks.why: Tachycardia, clamped skin, delayed refill and a narrowed pulse pressure of 22 mmHg are compensation succeeding at holding the systolic up. Decompensated shock would show a falling pressure and dropping mental status.

checks.q: Why does the diastolic pressure often rise before the systolic falls in early blood loss?
choices: The heart contracts harder during diastole
Vasoconstriction raises resistance, which raises the diastolic toward the systolic
Blood becomes thicker and pushes harder on vessel walls
Baroreceptors stop firing entirely
checks.why: Diastolic pressure largely reflects arteriolar resistance, so clamping vessels drives it up and narrows the pulse pressure. That narrowing is visible before the systolic ever moves.

checks.q: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 6-year-old?
choices: 90 mmHg
100 mmHg
82 mmHg
60 mmHg
checks.why: The formula 70 + (2 × age) gives 70 + 12 = 82 mmHg for a 6-year-old. Anything below that is decompensated and near arrest, since children hold pressure until very late.

lessons.title: Shock: one idea, four families
lessons.body:
## One definition, no number in it

**Shock is inadequate perfusion.** Cells are not getting enough oxygen and glucose, or cannot clear their `CO2`, regardless of what the blood pressure reads.

Notice what is missing from that sentence: a threshold. Shock is a state of the tissues, not a blood pressure value. A patient with a systolic of `130` can be in shock and a small, healthy adult with a systolic of `92` may be perfectly perfused.

Now reuse the pump-pipes-fluid-air frame. Perfusion can fail in exactly four ways, so there are exactly four families of shock.

> **Key:** Not enough fluid, pipes too wide, pump too weak, or something blocking flow. That is the entire list.

## 1. Hypovolemic — not enough fluid

The tank is low. Causes include bleeding (hemorrhagic shock) and non-bleeding losses: vomiting, diarrhea, burns, and severe dehydration.

Picture a fast weak pulse, pale cool clammy skin, thirst, a narrowing pulse pressure, and a source of loss you can usually find. Treatment is stopping the loss and replacing volume.

## 2. Distributive — pipes too wide

The tank is full but the container suddenly got much bigger, so there is not enough pressure to drive flow. Three versions matter.

- **Septic** — infection triggers body-wide vasodilation and leaky capillaries. Often warm and flushed early, then cold and mottled late.
- **Anaphylactic** — severe allergic reaction releases histamine: vasodilation, leaking, plus airway swelling and wheeze. Epinephrine `0.3 mg IM` in an adult (`0.15 mg` for a small child, per protocol) is the treatment precisely because it constricts vessels and opens airways at once.
- **Neurogenic** — spinal cord injury cuts the sympathetic signal below the level of injury. Vessels dilate and cannot constrict. Uniquely, the heart rate does **not** rise, and the skin below the injury is warm, pink and dry.

> **Trap:** Neurogenic shock is the one without a fast pulse and without cold clammy skin. If the only pattern you memorize is pale, cool, tachycardic, this case will slip past you.

## 3. Cardiogenic — the pump is too weak

The heart cannot squeeze hard enough. Usually a large heart attack, sometimes an arrhythmia or end-stage heart failure.

Picture low pressure plus signs of backup: crackles in the lungs, breathlessness, distended neck veins, swollen legs. Giving fluid tends to make it worse, and that is what separates it from hypovolemia at the bedside.

## 4. Obstructive — flow is physically blocked

Pump and volume are adequate, but something is in the way. Three to know:

- **Tension pneumothorax** — trapped air in the chest compresses the heart and great vessels
- **Cardiac tamponade** — blood in the sac around the heart prevents filling
- **Massive pulmonary embolism** — a clot blocks blood leaving the right heart

All three show shock with distended neck veins, and none of them improve until the obstruction itself is relieved.

## The thread

Every family ends at the same cellular problem: too little oxygen and glucose arriving. That is why the early signs overlap so heavily, and why naming the family, not just saying shock, is what actually changes treatment.

> **On the exam:** Warm, flushed and hypotensive points to distributive. Cold, clammy and hypotensive with lung crackles points to cardiogenic. Cold, clammy and hypotensive with an obvious loss points to hypovolemic. Shock with distended neck veins and clear lungs points to obstructive.
keyPoints: Shock is inadequate perfusion, defined by tissue state, not by a blood pressure number.
Four families: hypovolemic (fluid), distributive (pipes), cardiogenic (pump), obstructive (blocked flow).
Distributive includes septic, anaphylactic and neurogenic; adult anaphylaxis gets epinephrine 0.3 mg IM.
Neurogenic shock is warm, pink, dry skin without tachycardia.
Obstructive shock shows distended neck veins and does not improve until the obstruction is relieved.

checks.q: A 28-year-old with a cervical spine injury has BP 82/50, HR 62, and warm dry pink skin below the clavicles. Which shock family?
choices: Hypovolemic
Cardiogenic
Obstructive
Distributive, neurogenic type
checks.why: Loss of sympathetic outflow below the injury dilates vessels and removes the ability to speed the heart, giving hypotension with a normal or slow pulse and warm dry skin. Hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock both produce cold clammy skin with tachycardia.

checks.q: Which finding best separates cardiogenic shock from hypovolemic shock at the bedside?
choices: Crackles in the lungs and distended neck veins
A heart rate above 100
Pale, cool skin
Anxiety and restlessness
checks.why: Both families produce tachycardia, cool skin and anxiety. Only the failing pump backs blood up, giving pulmonary crackles and jugular venous distention, which also warns you that fluid will make it worse.

checks.q: A patient with shock, clear lung sounds and distended neck veins most likely has which family?
choices: Hypovolemic
Septic
Obstructive
Anaphylactic
checks.why: Distended neck veins with clear lungs means blood cannot get through or into the heart, as in tension pneumothorax, tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism. Hypovolemic and distributive shock produce flat neck veins because the vascular container is underfilled.

lessons.title: The eleven systems and what each one is for
lessons.body:
## Why systems are a useful simplification

The body is one continuous thing. Splitting it into eleven systems is a filing convention, and it earns its keep because most emergencies show up as one system failing loudly while the others compensate.

Learn each system by its job, not by its parts list. The job is what the patient loses when it fails.

## The eleven

| System | Job in one line | Failure looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Integumentary (skin) | Barrier, temperature control, sensation | Burns, infection, heat and cold emergencies |
| Skeletal | Structure, protection, blood cell production, calcium storage | Fractures, deformity, marrow disease |
| Muscular | Movement, posture, heat generation | Weakness, immobility, crush injury |
| Nervous | Sense, decide, command, in milliseconds | Altered mental status, stroke, seizure, paralysis |
| Endocrine | Chemical messengers over minutes to days | Diabetic emergencies, thyroid crisis, adrenal crisis |
| Cardiovascular | Move blood to every cell | Chest pain, shock, cardiac arrest |
| Lymphatic and immune | Drain tissue fluid, fight infection | Sepsis, anaphylaxis, swelling |
| Respiratory | Load oxygen, unload carbon dioxide | Shortness of breath, low `SpO2`, `CO2` retention |
| Digestive | Break food down, absorb fuel and water | Vomiting, abdominal pain, GI bleeding |
| Urinary | Filter blood, balance water, salt and acid | Retention, high potassium, uremia |
| Reproductive | Produce offspring | Obstetric emergency, vaginal or testicular emergency |

You will hear skeletal and muscular collapsed together as musculoskeletal, and lymphatic called the immune system. Both are fine.

## The three that keep you alive minute to minute

Respiratory, cardiovascular and nervous are the ones that kill in minutes. That is not an opinion, it is the same `4`–`6` minute clock from the first lesson. Everything else fails over hours to years.

This is why your primary assessment is essentially a rapid audit of those three systems and nothing else.

## Two speeds of control

Notice the nervous and endocrine systems do the same job by different clocks. The nervous system sends electrical signals down wires and gets an answer in milliseconds. The endocrine system releases hormones into blood and gets an answer in minutes to days.

Fast and precise versus slow and widespread. Adrenaline is the seam between them: it is released as a hormone from the adrenal glands and acts exactly like the sympathetic nerve signal.

> **Key:** Systems do not work alone. A respiratory problem becomes a nervous system problem in minutes, and a cardiovascular problem becomes a kidney problem in hours.

## Following one failure across systems

Take a severe pneumonia. The respiratory system fails first, so oxygen delivery drops. The cardiovascular system compensates with a faster pulse. The immune system floods the body with inflammatory signals, which dilates vessels and drops pressure into septic shock. Poor perfusion starves the kidneys, so urine output falls and acid builds. The rising acid and falling oxygen reach the brain, and the patient becomes confused.

One organ started it. Five systems are now involved, and the confusion that finally made the family call is the fifth domino, not the first.

> **On shift:** When a patient looks bad in a way you cannot name, ask which of the eleven is failing and what it was supposed to be doing. That question converts a vague impression into a working problem.
keyPoints: Eleven systems: integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic/immune, respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive.
Respiratory, cardiovascular and nervous are the three that kill within minutes.
The nervous system controls in milliseconds; the endocrine system controls in minutes to days.
Systems fail in chains, so the presenting complaint is often several dominoes down the line.
Naming the failing system and its job turns a vague impression into a workable problem.

checks.q: Which three systems make up the primary assessment because they kill within minutes?
choices: Respiratory, cardiovascular, nervous
Digestive, urinary, endocrine
Skeletal, muscular, integumentary
Lymphatic, reproductive, endocrine
checks.why: Airway and breathing are respiratory, circulation is cardiovascular, and disability is nervous. The other eight systems fail over hours to years, so they belong to the secondary assessment.

checks.q: What is the main difference between nervous and endocrine control?
choices: The nervous system uses hormones and the endocrine system uses nerves
The nervous system acts in milliseconds; the endocrine system acts over minutes to days
Only the endocrine system can affect the heart
The endocrine system works only during sleep
checks.why: Both are control systems, but one signals electrically along wires for speed and precision while the other releases hormones into the bloodstream for slower, widespread effects. Epinephrine sits at the seam and does both.

checks.q: A patient with severe pneumonia becomes confused. Which statement best describes what happened?
choices: The nervous system failed first and caused the pneumonia
Confusion is unrelated to the lung infection
Respiratory failure led to poor oxygen delivery and shock, and the brain is showing the result
The endocrine system caused the confusion directly
checks.why: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to low oxygen and rising acid, so it commonly announces failures that started elsewhere. Treating the confusion means fixing the oxygenation and perfusion problem behind it.

lessons.title: Two wires: sympathetic and parasympathetic
lessons.body:
## The part of you that runs itself

The nervous system splits into the part you command (somatic, such as moving your hand) and the part that runs without you (autonomic: heart rate, digestion, pupil size, sweating).

The autonomic half sends two opposing wires to most organs. Both are always active. What changes is which one is winning.

- **Sympathetic** — fight or flight. Spend energy now. Messengers: norepinephrine and epinephrine (adrenaline).
- **Parasympathetic** — rest and digest. Restore and store. Messenger: acetylcholine, carried mostly by the vagus nerve.

> **Key:** Sympathetic prepares you to run from a bear. Parasympathetic prepares you to nap after dinner. Every sign in the table below follows from that one image.

## Organ by organ

| Target | Sympathetic | Parasympathetic |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | Faster, up to `150` or more | Slower, can drop under `50` |
| Force of contraction | Stronger | Slightly weaker |
| Blood pressure | Up | Down |
| Arterioles in skin and gut | Constrict, so pale and cool | Normal tone |
| Sweat glands | Activate, so clammy | Quiet, so dry |
| Pupils | Dilate (mydriasis) | Constrict (miosis) |
| Bronchioles | Dilate, easier airflow | Constrict, wheeze |
| Gut motility | Slows or stops | Speeds up |
| Bladder | Holds | Empties |
| Liver | Releases glucose | Stores glucose |
| Salivation | Dry mouth | Watery |

Read the shock skin again with that table in hand: pale, cool, clammy, fast pulse, dilated pupils, dry mouth. That is not a mysterious syndrome. That is a maximal sympathetic surge, and it tells you the body has already decided it is in trouble.

## Why this table earns its keep

**Drugs.** Albuterol mimics sympathetic signaling at the lung to dilate bronchioles, and its side effects are a fast pulse and tremor because the same wire runs to the heart. Epinephrine `0.3 mg IM` for anaphylaxis constricts vessels, opens bronchioles and speeds the heart, three rows of the table in one syringe. Beta blockers such as metoprolol cut sympathetic drive, which is why a patient taking one may be unable to mount the fast pulse you expect in shock. Atropine `1 mg IV` blocks the parasympathetic brake to raise a dangerously slow heart rate.

**Poisonings.** Organophosphate pesticide exposure floods the body with parasympathetic signal: pinpoint pupils, drooling, tearing, urination, diarrhea, vomiting, wheezing and a slow heart. Stimulant overdose does the opposite: wide pupils, hot skin, racing pulse, agitation.

**Reflexes.** The vagus nerve is the parasympathetic brake on the heart. Straining on the toilet, vomiting, or suctioning the back of the throat too deeply can fire it and drop heart rate and pressure hard. A person can faint from a vagal surge with nothing else wrong.

> **Trap:** A normal heart rate in an obviously sick patient does not rule out shock. Beta blockers, pacemakers, and spinal cord injury all remove the ability to speed up.

> **On shift:** Pinpoint pupils raise two questions: opioids, or a cholinergic exposure such as organophosphates? Both shrink pupils. The rest of the exam, especially the wet secretions, separates them.
keyPoints: Sympathetic spends energy (fast pulse, dilated pupils, pale clammy skin, open bronchioles, quiet gut).
Parasympathetic restores (slow pulse, pinpoint pupils, dry warm skin, constricted bronchioles, active gut).
Shock skin is simply a maximal sympathetic surge you can read without equipment.
Beta blockers, pacemakers and spinal injury can block the expected tachycardia in shock.
Vagal stimulation from straining, vomiting or deep suctioning can drop heart rate and pressure.

checks.q: Which set of findings is a pure sympathetic surge?
choices: Pinpoint pupils, drooling, slow pulse, wheeze
Dilated pupils, fast pulse, pale clammy skin, dry mouth
Warm dry skin, normal pulse, normal pupils
Flushed face, slow pulse, watery eyes
checks.why: Fight or flight dilates pupils, speeds and strengthens the heart, clamps skin vessels while turning on sweat glands, and shuts down salivation. The pinpoint-and-wet pattern is the opposite wire, the parasympathetic one.

checks.q: A 68-year-old on metoprolol has BP 84/58 with pale clammy skin but a heart rate of 74. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The heart rate rules out shock
The beta blocker is blunting the expected tachycardia, so judge perfusion on the other findings
The blood pressure reading must be wrong
Metoprolol causes pale clammy skin as a side effect
checks.why: Beta blockers block the sympathetic signal to the heart, so the compensatory tachycardia never appears even in real shock. The hypotension and the clamped skin are the reliable findings here.

checks.q: Why does deep suctioning of the throat sometimes cause a sudden drop in heart rate?
choices: It removes oxygen from the airway
It stimulates the vagus nerve, which is the parasympathetic brake on the heart
It triggers a sympathetic surge
It lowers blood glucose
checks.why: Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine at the heart and slows it, which is why suction attempts are kept brief and the patient is monitored. Suctioning does also remove oxygen, but the bradycardia itself is the vagal reflex.

lessons.title: Acid and base without the chemistry class
lessons.body:
## pH in plain language

pH measures how acidic a fluid is. Blood is held remarkably tight, between `7.35` and `7.45`. Under `7.35` is acidosis, over `7.45` is alkalosis. Outside roughly `6.8` to `7.8`, enzymes stop working and the patient dies.

The band is narrow because proteins change shape when pH changes, and every enzyme, every receptor, and hemoglobin itself is a protein. Wrong shape means wrong function.

## Two acids, two exits

The body produces acid all day and disposes of it two ways.

1. **Carbonic acid, which comes from `CO2`** — leaves through the **lungs** in seconds to minutes. This is the fast dial.
2. **Metabolic acids such as lactic acid and ketones** — leave through the **kidneys** over hours to days. This is the slow dial.

The link is one reaction worth knowing in words: `CO2` plus water makes carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion plus bicarbonate. Add `CO2` and you push the reaction toward more acid. Remove `CO2` and acid falls.

> **Key:** More `CO2` means more acid, less `CO2` means less acid, and the lungs can move that dial faster than anything else in the body.

## The four buckets

| Problem | What started it | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| Respiratory acidosis | Not blowing off `CO2` | Opioid overdose, COPD, airway obstruction |
| Respiratory alkalosis | Blowing off too much `CO2` | Panic, pain, early sepsis, high altitude |
| Metabolic acidosis | Too much acid or lost bicarbonate | Shock, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe diarrhea |
| Metabolic alkalosis | Lost acid or gained bicarbonate | Prolonged vomiting, antacid overuse |

The naming rule is simple. If the `CO2` caused the problem, it is respiratory. If something else caused it, it is metabolic.

## Why breathing fast fixes acidosis

A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is drowning in ketone acid. The kidneys are far too slow to help in the next hour, so the brainstem cranks respirations up into deep, fast, sighing breaths called **Kussmaul respirations**, blowing off `CO2` and pulling pH back up.

The same correction runs quietly in shock. Lactic acid builds and the patient breathes faster. That tachypnea is chemistry, not anxiety, and if you suppress it, for example by oversedating, the pH falls off a cliff.

This is also the mechanism behind a respiratory rate of `28` being an early sepsis flag while the blood pressure still looks fine.

> **Trap:** Fast breathing in a sick patient is usually the compensation, not the problem. Ask what acid it is clearing before you try to slow it.

## Why vomiting causes alkalosis

Stomach contents are strongly acidic, with a gastric pH around `1.5` to `3.5`. Repeated vomiting throws hydrochloric acid out of the body. Remove acid and what remains is relatively alkaline. That is metabolic alkalosis, and it is why a patient with three days of vomiting can arrive with a blood pH of `7.50`.

Diarrhea does the opposite. Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate, which is base, so losing it from below causes metabolic acidosis.

## The direction the body pushes

Compensation always aims at the opposite direction of the primary problem, and it never fully corrects. A metabolic acidosis gets respiratory compensation, meaning fast breathing. A respiratory acidosis gets renal compensation, meaning the kidneys keep more bicarbonate over a day or two.

> **On the exam:** Vomiting equals alkalosis. Diarrhea equals acidosis. The direction follows whichever end you are losing fluid from.
keyPoints: Normal blood pH is 7.35–7.45; lungs clear acid in minutes, kidneys over hours to days.
More CO2 means more acid; blowing off CO2 raises pH.
Four buckets: respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis.
Kussmaul respirations in DKA are the lungs compensating for metabolic acidosis, not the problem.
Vomiting loses acid and causes alkalosis; diarrhea loses bicarbonate and causes acidosis.

checks.q: An opioid overdose patient is breathing 6 times a minute. What acid-base problem develops?
choices: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
checks.why: Slow shallow breathing retains CO2, which forms carbonic acid and drops pH, so the disorder is respiratory and acidotic. Ventilating the patient is the direct fix because the lungs are the fast dial.

checks.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 32 per minute. What should you do with that rate?
choices: Sedate the patient to slow the breathing
Recognize it as compensation for metabolic acidosis and support it
Assume anxiety and offer reassurance only
Apply a non-rebreather to slow the drive
checks.why: Kussmaul respirations are the body blowing off CO2 to offset ketone acid, and removing that drive causes the pH to crash. The underlying fix is fluids and insulin, not slowing the respirations.

checks.q: Three days of persistent vomiting produces which disorder, and why?
choices: Metabolic acidosis, because the stomach loses bicarbonate
Respiratory alkalosis, because vomiting increases the respiratory rate
Metabolic alkalosis, because hydrochloric acid is lost from the body
Respiratory acidosis, because vomiting obstructs the airway
checks.why: Gastric fluid has a pH around 1.5 to 3.5, so vomiting it out removes acid and leaves the blood relatively alkaline. Losing fluid from the other end, where it is bicarbonate-rich, produces the opposite result.

lessons.title: Cells to systems, and what organ failure means
lessons.body:
## Four floors

Biology stacks in levels, and each floor is the one below it organized for a purpose.

1. **Cells** — the smallest living unit. A cardiac muscle cell contracts, a neuron signals, a red blood cell carries oxygen.
2. **Tissues** — many similar cells doing one job together. Four types: epithelial (covers and lines), connective (binds and supports, including blood and bone), muscle (contracts), and nervous (conducts).
3. **Organs** — different tissues built into a structure with a job. A stomach has an epithelial lining, a muscular wall, connective layers, and its own nerve supply.
4. **Organ systems** — organs cooperating on a larger job, such as the digestive system moving food from mouth to waste.

> **Key:** Every system failure you will ever treat started as cells not receiving oxygen and glucose. The levels only tell you how far the damage has spread.

## What organ failure actually means

An organ fails when it can no longer do its job well enough to keep the rest of the body in balance. That is a functional statement, not an anatomic one. The organ is still sitting there.

Failure comes in two speeds. **Acute** failure develops over minutes to days and is often reversible if perfusion and oxygenation are restored quickly. **Chronic** failure develops over months to years, and the body has adapted around it, which is why a patient with chronic kidney failure walks around with numbers that would kill someone else this week.

## Named failures worth knowing

- **Respiratory failure** — the lungs cannot oxygenate, cannot ventilate, or both. Rising `CO2` makes the patient sleepy, and that sleepiness is an emergency, not an improvement.
- **Heart failure** — the pump cannot keep up, so blood backs up behind it. Left-sided backup floods the lungs: crackles and breathlessness. Right-sided backup floods the body: leg swelling and distended neck veins.
- **Kidney failure** — filtering stops, so potassium, acid and fluid build. A potassium above roughly `6.5 mEq/L` can stop the heart.
- **Liver failure** — no detoxification, no clotting factors, no protein production. Patients bleed, swell, turn yellow (jaundice), and become confused.
- **Brain failure** — anything from mild confusion to coma, described with AVPU or scored with the Glasgow Coma Scale from `3` to `15`.

## The cascade

Organs do not fail politely, one at a time. Prolonged shock starves several at once, and failure in one poisons the others. The combined state is called multiple organ dysfunction syndrome.

A common chain: sustained low perfusion starves the kidneys; failing kidneys let potassium and acid build; acidosis weakens the heart's contraction; the weaker pump drops perfusion further. Once that loop is turning, mortality climbs steeply with every additional organ involved.

The practical lesson is about timing. Reversing one failing organ is realistic. Reversing four that are feeding each other usually is not.

> **Trap:** By the time an organ is visibly failing, the insult usually happened hours earlier. The moment to intervene is when the only findings are a fast pulse and cool skin.

> **On shift:** Assessment follows the clock, not the anatomy. Restore oxygen and flow first; the organ-by-organ workup comes after the patient is no longer dying.
keyPoints: Levels of organization: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems.
The four tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Organ failure is functional, not anatomic, and comes in acute and chronic speeds.
Left heart failure backs blood into the lungs; right heart failure backs it into the body.
Multiple organ dysfunction is a self-feeding loop, so intervene while the findings are still subtle.

checks.q: Which sequence correctly orders the levels of organization?
choices: Tissues, cells, systems, organs
Cells, tissues, organs, organ systems
Organs, cells, tissues, systems
Cells, organs, tissues, systems
checks.why: Similar cells form tissues, different tissues combine into organs, and cooperating organs form systems. Each level is the one below it organized for a job.

checks.q: A patient has crackles in both lung bases and severe shortness of breath when lying flat. Which side of the heart is backing up?
choices: The left side, because blood backs up into the lungs
The right side, because blood backs up into the lungs
Neither side; this is a kidney problem
Both sides equally, always
checks.why: The left ventricle receives blood from the lungs, so when it fails, pressure backs up into pulmonary vessels and fluid leaks into alveoli. Right-sided failure instead backs blood into the body, producing leg swelling and distended neck veins.

checks.q: Why is multiple organ dysfunction syndrome so lethal?
choices: Because each failing organ is treated separately and never interacts
Because failure in one organ worsens the others in a self-feeding loop
Because it only occurs in patients with chronic disease
Because it always begins in the liver
checks.why: Kidney failure raises acid and potassium, which weakens the heart, which lowers perfusion, which damages more organs. Mortality rises sharply with each organ added, which is why early perfusion restoration matters more than late organ-specific care.

cards.front: What two things must reach every cell, and what must leave?
cards.back: Oxygen and glucose in, carbon dioxide out. Every airway, breathing and circulation problem is a failure of that one delivery job.

cards.front: How much ATP comes from one glucose with oxygen versus without?
cards.back: With oxygen (aerobic): about 30–32 ATP. Without oxygen (anaerobic): 2 ATP plus lactic acid, roughly six percent of the yield.

cards.front: Why does low blood sugar change mental status so fast?
cards.back: Brain cells run almost entirely on glucose and store almost none. Under 70 mg/dL with symptoms is hypoglycemia, and it can perfectly mimic stroke or intoxication.

cards.front: What does retained CO2 do to blood pH?
cards.back: CO2 dissolves into carbonic acid, so retaining it lowers pH toward acidosis. Blowing CO2 off raises pH toward alkalosis.

cards.front: How long does the brain tolerate no oxygen before damage begins?
cards.back: About 4–6 minutes. Heart muscle tolerates 20–30 minutes, kidney 30–60 minutes, skeletal muscle 2–4 hours.

cards.front: What waste product marks anaerobic metabolism, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Lactic acid. It accumulates during poor perfusion and produces metabolic acidosis well before blood pressure falls, so it is an early chemistry sign of shock.

cards.front: Define perfusion in one sentence.
cards.back: Blood actually reaching tissue and exchanging oxygen, glucose and CO2 with it. Having a blood pressure is not the same as perfusing.

cards.front: What are the four requirements for perfusion?
cards.back: Pump (heart), pipes (vessels), fluid (blood volume) and air (lung gas exchange). Each shock family is one of these four failing.

cards.front: What is the cardiac output equation and the normal adult resting value?
cards.back: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. About 70 mL × 70 beats/min, so roughly 5 L per minute at rest.

cards.front: Normal adult stroke volume and total blood volume?
cards.back: Stroke volume 60–100 mL per beat. Total blood volume about 5 L, roughly 70 mL/kg of body weight.

cards.front: How can a patient be in shock without losing a drop of blood?
cards.back: Vasodilation widens the pipes, so the same volume no longer fills the larger container and pressure falls. That is distributive shock.

cards.front: Name five bedside windows onto perfusion.
cards.back: Skin color, temperature and moisture; capillary refill under 2 seconds; mental status; urine output with a floor of 0.5 mL/kg/hr; and pulse quality.

cards.front: How much blood must an adult lose before blood pressure falls?
cards.back: About 15 percent, roughly 750 mL, is tolerated with little change. Pressure generally falls around 30–40 percent loss, meaning 1.5–2 L.

cards.front: What is the difference between oxygenation and ventilation?
cards.back: Oxygenation is loading oxygen into blood. Ventilation is moving air in and out to clear CO2. A patient can fail at either one alone.

cards.front: Why is the ABC order a chain rather than a preference?
cards.back: Each step is useless without the one before it. An open airway does nothing without breathing, and breathing does nothing without circulation to carry the oxygen.

cards.front: What most commonly blocks the airway in an unconscious adult lying face up?
cards.back: The tongue falling back against the throat after muscle tone is lost. A head-tilt chin-lift, or jaw-thrust if spine injury is suspected, usually fixes it.

cards.front: How much of each adult breath is anatomic dead space, and why does it matter?
cards.back: About 150 mL fills the trachea and bronchi and never reaches alveoli. Very shallow breaths mostly refill dead space, so fast and shallow can move almost no useful air.

cards.front: What is the one finding that comes before airway?
cards.back: Catastrophic external hemorrhage. A torn femoral artery can empty an adult in under 3 minutes, faster than an airway problem kills.

cards.front: What does the D in the primary assessment cover?
cards.back: Disability, meaning the brain: level of consciousness, pupils, movement and sensation in all four limbs, and blood glucose.

cards.front: Why re-cover a patient after exposing them for examination?
cards.back: A cold patient clots poorly and bleeds more. Hypothermia worsens coagulation and acidosis, so exposure should be quick and followed by warming.

cards.front: What is homeostasis, and what are the three parts of every control loop?
cards.back: Holding internal values inside a narrow band. Every loop has a sensor detecting drift, a control center comparing to a set point, and an effector pushing back.

cards.front: Why does heart rate rise before blood pressure falls?
cards.back: Cardiac output is stroke volume times rate. When stroke volume drops, raising rate holds output and pressure steady, so tachycardia appears first.

cards.front: What three moves does the sympathetic system make to defend blood pressure?
cards.back: Raise heart rate, raise contractility so each squeeze is harder, and constrict arterioles in skin, gut and muscle to raise resistance.

cards.front: Why is shock skin pale, cool and clammy?
cards.back: Vasoconstriction pulls blood out of the skin to protect brain, heart and kidneys, giving pale cool skin, while the same sympathetic surge turns on sweat glands.

cards.front: Normal pulse pressure, and what a narrowing one means?
cards.back: Systolic minus diastolic, normally 30–40 mmHg. Narrowing means arterioles are clamping and is an early hypovolemia sign, as in 120/80 becoming 118/96.

cards.front: Compensated versus decompensated shock in one line each?
cards.back: Compensated: perfusion already inadequate but pressure held up by fast pulse and clamped vessels. Decompensated: defenses fail, pressure falls, mental status drops. Late and near arrest.

cards.front: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure for a child aged 1 to 10?
cards.back: 70 + (2 × age in years). For a 6-year-old that is 82 mmHg. Below it, the child is decompensated and near arrest.

cards.front: Why do children crash suddenly after looking stable?
cards.back: They compensate hard and can lose 30–40 percent of blood volume with a normal pressure, then exhaust the reserve all at once. Hypotension in a child is a pre-arrest finding.

cards.front: Define shock without using a blood pressure number.
cards.back: Inadequate perfusion: cells are not receiving enough oxygen and glucose or cannot clear CO2. It is a tissue state, not a pressure threshold.

cards.front: Name the four families of shock and the failure behind each.
cards.back: Hypovolemic (not enough fluid), distributive (pipes too wide), cardiogenic (pump too weak), obstructive (flow physically blocked).

cards.front: What are the three types of distributive shock?
cards.back: Septic from infection, anaphylactic from severe allergic reaction, and neurogenic from spinal cord injury cutting sympathetic outflow.

cards.front: What makes neurogenic shock look different from every other kind?
cards.back: No tachycardia and no cold clammy skin. Skin below the injury is warm, pink and dry because sympathetic signal is cut and vessels cannot constrict.

cards.front: Adult epinephrine dose for anaphylaxis, and why epinephrine specifically?
cards.back: 0.3 mg IM in the lateral thigh (0.15 mg for a small child, per protocol). It constricts vessels and dilates bronchioles at the same time.

cards.front: Which findings separate cardiogenic shock from hypovolemic shock?
cards.back: Signs of backup: lung crackles, distended neck veins and leg swelling. Both look cold, clammy and tachycardic otherwise, but fluid worsens cardiogenic shock.

cards.front: What are the three causes of obstructive shock?
cards.back: Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, and massive pulmonary embolism. All three show distended neck veins and do not improve until the obstruction is relieved.

cards.front: Shock with distended neck veins and clear lung sounds points to what?
cards.back: Obstructive shock, especially tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism. Hypovolemic and distributive shock give flat neck veins; cardiogenic usually gives crackles.

cards.front: List the eleven body systems.
cards.back: Integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic and immune, respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive.

cards.front: Which three systems are the primary assessment, and why those three?
cards.back: Respiratory, cardiovascular and nervous. They are the only ones that kill within the 4–6 minute brain clock; the other eight fail over hours to years.

cards.front: How do the nervous and endocrine systems differ in speed and reach?
cards.back: The nervous system signals electrically in milliseconds with precise targets. The endocrine system releases hormones into blood for effects over minutes to days, body-wide.

cards.front: What is the urinary system's job beyond making urine?
cards.back: Filtering blood and balancing water, salt and acid. When it fails, potassium, acid and fluid build up, which is why kidney failure endangers the heart.

cards.front: Why is the confusion in a septic pneumonia patient a late sign?
cards.back: It is the fifth domino. Lungs fail, the heart compensates, inflammation dilates vessels, perfusion drops, and only then does the brain show the result.

cards.front: What is the integumentary system responsible for?
cards.back: Barrier against infection, temperature regulation, fluid retention and sensation. Burns fail all four at once, which is why they cause fluid loss and infection risk.

cards.front: What is the one-line difference between sympathetic and parasympathetic?
cards.back: Sympathetic is fight or flight, spending energy now. Parasympathetic is rest and digest, restoring and storing. Both wires run to most organs at all times.

cards.front: What does the sympathetic system do to pulse, blood pressure, pupils, skin and gut?
cards.back: Pulse faster and stronger, pressure up, pupils dilate, skin pale cool and clammy, gut motility slows or stops.

cards.front: What does the parasympathetic system do to pulse, pupils, bronchioles and gut?
cards.back: Pulse slower, pupils constrict to pinpoint, bronchioles constrict and can wheeze, gut motility and secretions increase. Carried mainly by the vagus nerve.

cards.front: Why does albuterol cause tremor and a fast pulse?
cards.back: It mimics sympathetic signaling to dilate bronchioles, and the same signaling pathway runs to the heart and skeletal muscle, producing tachycardia and tremor.

cards.front: Name three reasons a shock patient might not be tachycardic.
cards.back: Beta blockers such as metoprolol, an implanted pacemaker, and spinal cord injury cutting sympathetic outflow. Judge perfusion on skin, mental status and pressure instead.

cards.front: What does organophosphate poisoning look like, and which wire is it?
cards.back: A parasympathetic flood: pinpoint pupils, drooling, tearing, urination, diarrhea, vomiting, wheezing, slow heart. Everything gets wet and slow.

cards.front: Normal blood pH range, and which organ moves it fastest?
cards.back: 7.35 to 7.45. The lungs move it in seconds to minutes by changing CO2; the kidneys take hours to days using bicarbonate.

cards.front: How does CO2 turn into acid?
cards.back: CO2 plus water forms carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate. More CO2 means more acid and a lower pH.

cards.front: Name the four acid-base buckets with one cause each.
cards.back: Respiratory acidosis (opioid overdose), respiratory alkalosis (panic), metabolic acidosis (shock or DKA), metabolic alkalosis (prolonged vomiting).

cards.front: What are Kussmaul respirations and what are they doing?
cards.back: Deep, fast, sighing breaths seen in diabetic ketoacidosis. They blow off CO2 to offset metabolic acid, so they are compensation, not the primary problem.

cards.front: Why does vomiting cause alkalosis but diarrhea cause acidosis?
cards.back: Gastric fluid has a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5, so vomiting removes acid. Intestinal fluid is bicarbonate-rich, so diarrhea removes base.

cards.front: What are the four levels of organization and the four tissue types?
cards.back: Levels: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems. Tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.

cards.front: What does organ failure actually mean?
cards.back: The organ can no longer do its job well enough to keep the body in balance. It is functional, not anatomic, and comes in acute and chronic speeds.

cards.front: Left-sided versus right-sided heart failure: where does blood back up?
cards.back: Left-sided backs up into the lungs, giving crackles and breathlessness. Right-sided backs up into the body, giving leg swelling and distended neck veins.

cards.front: Why does kidney failure threaten the heart?
cards.back: Filtering stops, so potassium and acid accumulate. A potassium above roughly 6.5 mEq/L can cause lethal rhythms, and acidosis weakens contraction.

cards.front: Why is multiple organ dysfunction syndrome so hard to reverse?
cards.back: Failures feed each other: poor perfusion harms kidneys, rising acid and potassium weaken the heart, the weaker pump lowers perfusion further. Mortality climbs with every organ added.

quiz.q: A cell is deprived of oxygen but still has glucose available. Which statement best describes what happens next?
choices: Metabolism stops completely within seconds
The cell produces the same amount of ATP through a backup pathway
The cell produces about 2 ATP per glucose and releases lactic acid
The cell begins to consume carbon dioxide for energy
quiz.why: Anaerobic metabolism still splits glucose but yields only 2 ATP instead of the 30–32 available with oxygen, and the byproduct is lactic acid. Metabolism does not stop instantly, and no pathway matches aerobic yield without oxygen.

quiz.q: A 54-year-old is found confused and sweating. His partner says he takes insulin. What single test most likely explains everything you are seeing?
choices: Blood glucose by fingerstick
Pulse oximetry
Oral temperature
Blood pressure in both arms
quiz.why: The brain runs almost exclusively on glucose and stores none, so hypoglycemia produces confusion and diaphoresis within minutes and is instantly reversible. The other measurements are useful but none of them explain the whole picture in a known insulin user.

quiz.q: How long can the brain tolerate complete absence of oxygen before damage begins?
choices: 30 seconds
20 to 30 minutes
Over an hour
4 to 6 minutes
quiz.why: The 4–6 minute window is the entire reason for rapid CPR and airway management. Heart muscle tolerates 20–30 minutes and kidney 30–60 minutes, so those figures belong to other tissues.

quiz.q: A patient's stroke volume falls from 70 mL to 45 mL after significant blood loss. Which compensation keeps cardiac output near normal?
choices: Slowing the heart rate to allow better filling
Increasing the heart rate
Increasing the respiratory rate alone
Dilating the arterioles to reduce workload
quiz.why: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate, so fewer milliliters per beat is offset by more beats per minute. Slowing the rate would lower output further, and dilating arterioles would drop pressure, which is the opposite of compensation.

quiz.q: Which patient best illustrates shock caused by the pipes rather than the fluid?
choices: A patient with a peanut allergy who is hypotensive, flushed and wheezing after eating
A patient hypotensive after vomiting for three days
A patient hypotensive with a femur fracture and a large thigh hematoma
A patient hypotensive with crackles after a large heart attack
quiz.why: Anaphylaxis releases histamine, which dilates vessels so the same volume cannot fill a larger container, and that is distributive shock. Vomiting and hematoma are volume losses, and the post-infarction patient has a pump problem.

quiz.q: An adult weighing 70 kg has an estimated total blood volume closest to which value?
choices: 1 liter
3 liters
5 liters
10 liters
quiz.why: Adult blood volume is roughly 70 mL/kg, so 70 kg gives about 4,900 mL, or 5 liters. That is also the approximate amount the heart moves every minute at rest, which makes the number easy to anchor.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has spurting bright red blood from the upper thigh and is making snoring sounds. What do you do first?
choices: Open the airway with a jaw-thrust
Apply direct pressure and a tourniquet to the thigh
Obtain a full set of vital signs
Apply high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather
quiz.why: Catastrophic external hemorrhage is the single exception that precedes airway, because an arterial bleed can empty an adult in under 3 minutes while airway obstruction takes 4–6. You return to the airway immediately after the bleeding is controlled.

quiz.q: Which adult is moving the least effective air despite an alarming respiratory rate?
choices: 22 breaths per minute with normal depth
14 breaths per minute with normal depth
18 breaths per minute with deep excursions
42 breaths per minute with barely visible chest rise
quiz.why: Each very shallow breath mostly refills the approximately 150 mL of anatomic dead space and never reaches the alveoli, so minute alveolar ventilation collapses. The other three all pair an acceptable rate with adequate depth.

quiz.q: Why is an unconscious adult lying supine at high risk for airway obstruction?
choices: Loss of muscle tone allows the tongue to fall back against the posterior pharynx
The alveoli collapse when a person lies flat
Gravity pulls blood away from the lungs
The diaphragm cannot move in the supine position
quiz.why: The tongue is anchored to the mandible, and without tone it falls backward and occludes the airway, which is corrected by a head-tilt chin-lift or jaw-thrust. The other options describe changes that do not obstruct the upper airway.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old involved in a motorcycle crash has HR 126, BP 116/94, RR 24, cool pale skin and capillary refill of 4 seconds. How should this be classified?
choices: Not in shock, because blood pressure is within normal limits
Decompensated hypovolemic shock
Compensated shock
Neurogenic shock
quiz.why: Tachycardia, tachypnea, clamped skin, delayed refill and a pulse pressure narrowed to 22 mmHg show compensation succeeding at holding the systolic up. Decompensation would show a falling pressure, and neurogenic shock produces warm dry skin without tachycardia.

quiz.q: What does a blood pressure that has begun to fall in a bleeding adult tell you?
choices: Shock is just beginning
The patient has lost roughly 10 percent of blood volume
Compensation is working well
Compensation has already failed and the patient is decompensated
quiz.why: Pressure is the last value to move because rate and vessel tone defend it; adults typically hold systolic until about 30 percent volume loss. A falling pressure therefore marks the end of compensation, not its start.

quiz.q: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 4-year-old?
choices: 90 mmHg
78 mmHg
60 mmHg
100 mmHg
quiz.why: For children aged 1 to 10, use 70 + (2 × age in years), so 70 + 8 gives 78 mmHg. Anything lower is decompensated, which in a child means near arrest because they hold pressure until very late.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with two days of vomiting and diarrhea is now quiet and limp after screaming on arrival. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Worsening perfusion to the brain as compensation fails
The child has calmed down and is improving
The child is sleeping normally for that age
Pain medication given earlier is taking effect
quiz.why: Children compensate hard and then fail abruptly, so a sudden change from vigorous to quiet and floppy signals a brain losing perfusion. Interpreting the change as calming is the classic and dangerous error in pediatric assessment.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old with a cervical spine fracture has BP 80/48, HR 58, and warm dry pink skin. Which shock family fits best?
choices: Hypovolemic shock from occult bleeding
Cardiogenic shock
Obstructive shock from tamponade
Distributive shock, neurogenic type
quiz.why: Cutting sympathetic outflow below the injury dilates vessels and removes the ability to raise heart rate, so the patient is hypotensive with a normal or slow pulse and warm dry skin. Every other family in this list produces cold clammy skin with tachycardia.

quiz.q: Which combination of findings most strongly suggests obstructive shock?
choices: Hypotension, flushed warm skin, fever
Hypotension, cool clammy skin, external bleeding
Hypotension, distended neck veins, clear lung sounds
Hypotension, bradycardia, warm dry skin below the nipple line
quiz.why: Blood cannot return to or leave the heart, so pressure backs up into the neck veins while lungs stay clear, as in tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism. Flushed and febrile suggests septic, bleeding suggests hypovolemic, and the last pattern is neurogenic.

quiz.q: An adult develops hives, throat tightness, wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/40 minutes after eating shellfish. What is the definitive early treatment?
choices: Albuterol by nebulizer alone
Epinephrine 0.3 mg intramuscularly in the lateral thigh
Diphenhydramine by mouth
A 1-liter fluid bolus alone
quiz.why: Epinephrine constricts dilated vessels and dilates bronchioles simultaneously, which is exactly what anaphylaxis requires, and it is the only listed option that addresses the hypotension. Albuterol, antihistamines and fluids are adjuncts that do not reverse the vasodilation fast enough.

quiz.q: Which finding most reliably distinguishes cardiogenic shock from hypovolemic shock in the field?
choices: Heart rate above 110
Cool, pale skin
Anxiety and restlessness
Crackles in the lungs with distended neck veins
quiz.why: Both families produce tachycardia, cool skin and anxiety, so those cannot separate them. Only a failing pump backs blood up behind it, producing pulmonary crackles and jugular distention, which also warns that a fluid bolus will worsen the patient.

quiz.q: Which three systems constitute the primary assessment because failure in any of them kills within minutes?
choices: Respiratory, cardiovascular, nervous
Endocrine, urinary, digestive
Skeletal, muscular, integumentary
Lymphatic, reproductive, integumentary
quiz.why: Airway and breathing are respiratory, circulation is cardiovascular, and disability is nervous, all governed by the 4–6 minute brain clock. The other eight systems fail over hours to years and belong to the secondary assessment.

quiz.q: A patient with pneumonia becomes hypotensive, then oliguric, then confused over six hours. What pattern does this illustrate?
choices: Three unrelated conditions occurring by coincidence
One system failure cascading into several others through poor perfusion
A primary neurologic event with a secondary pneumonia
A chronic process that has been present for months
quiz.why: Respiratory failure and inflammation lower perfusion, low perfusion starves kidneys so urine output falls, and rising acid with low oxygen finally reaches the brain. Recognizing the chain tells you to treat perfusion rather than chasing each organ in isolation.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly contrasts nervous and endocrine control?
choices: The endocrine system is faster because hormones travel in blood
Only the nervous system can influence heart rate
The nervous system acts in milliseconds, while the endocrine system acts over minutes to days
Both systems act on identical timescales
quiz.why: Electrical signaling along nerves is fast and precisely targeted, while hormones released into blood act slowly and body-wide. Epinephrine bridges both, acting as a hormone from the adrenal glands and as a sympathetic neurotransmitter.

quiz.q: Which set of signs represents a maximal sympathetic response?
choices: Dilated pupils, tachycardia, pale clammy skin, dry mouth
Pinpoint pupils, bradycardia, drooling, wheeze
Normal pupils, normal pulse, warm dry skin
Constricted pupils, flushed face, increased bowel sounds
quiz.why: Fight or flight dilates pupils, speeds and strengthens the heart, constricts skin vessels while activating sweat glands, and shuts down salivation and gut activity. The pinpoint-and-wet picture is a cholinergic, parasympathetic pattern.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old on metoprolol has BP 82/54, capillary refill of 5 seconds, pale clammy skin and HR 70. What is the best interpretation?
choices: A heart rate of 70 excludes shock
The blood pressure cuff is almost certainly malfunctioning
Metoprolol directly causes pale clammy skin
Beta blockade is masking the expected tachycardia, so the other findings define the picture
quiz.why: Beta blockers prevent the sympathetic signal from raising heart rate, so the usual compensatory tachycardia never appears even in genuine shock. Hypotension, delayed refill and clamped skin remain reliable and are enough to act on.

quiz.q: A farm worker is found with pinpoint pupils, copious drooling and tearing, vomiting, wheezing and a heart rate of 46. Which mechanism explains this?
choices: Massive sympathetic discharge
Overwhelming parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation, as from organophosphates
Complete loss of all autonomic tone
Isolated failure of the endocrine system
quiz.why: Every finding is a parasympathetic effect turned up at once: pupil constriction, secretions, gut activity, bronchoconstriction and bradycardia. A sympathetic surge would produce the opposite picture of wide pupils, dry skin and tachycardia.

quiz.q: An opioid overdose patient is breathing 5 times a minute. Which acid-base disturbance is developing?
choices: Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis from ketones
quiz.why: Hypoventilation retains CO2, which combines with water to form carbonic acid and lowers pH, making the problem respiratory and acidotic. Supporting ventilation corrects it directly because the lungs are the fastest acid-base dial the body has.

quiz.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 34 per minute. What is the correct interpretation of that respiratory rate?
choices: Primary respiratory failure requiring immediate sedation
Anxiety that should be treated with reassurance and coaching to slow down
An unrelated finding with no bearing on the metabolic problem
Kussmaul respirations compensating for metabolic acidosis, which must be supported
quiz.why: The lungs are blowing off CO2 to offset ketone acid because the kidneys are far too slow to help within the hour. Suppressing that drive causes the pH to fall rapidly; the real treatment is fluids and insulin for the underlying acidosis.

quiz.q: A patient has vomited repeatedly for three days and arrives with a blood pH of 7.51. Which disorder is present and why?
choices: Metabolic alkalosis, because hydrochloric acid was lost from the stomach
Metabolic acidosis, because the stomach is rich in bicarbonate
Respiratory acidosis, because vomiting obstructs the airway
Respiratory alkalosis, because vomiting raises the respiratory rate
quiz.why: Gastric fluid has a pH of roughly 1.5 to 3.5, so removing it from the body leaves the blood relatively alkaline. Fluid lost from the other end is bicarbonate-rich, which is why prolonged diarrhea causes the opposite disturbance.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly describes the levels of biological organization?
choices: Organs, cells, tissues, systems
Cells, tissues, organs, organ systems
Tissues, cells, organs, systems
Cells, organs, tissues, systems
quiz.why: Similar cells combine into tissues, different tissues combine into organs, and cooperating organs form systems. Each level is simply the level below it organized to accomplish a specific job.

quiz.q: A patient in prolonged shock develops rising potassium, worsening acidosis and a weakening heart. What is this pattern called and what does it imply?
choices: An isolated kidney injury with a good prognosis
A purely respiratory problem requiring only oxygen
Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, a self-feeding loop with steeply rising mortality
Chronic organ failure that the body has adapted to
quiz.why: Hypoperfusion injures the kidneys, retained potassium and acid weaken cardiac contraction, and the weaker pump lowers perfusion further, closing the loop. Chronic failure is the opposite situation, in which adaptation has occurred over months or years.

scenarios.title: Classroom: which system failed first?
scenarios.intro:
You are handed a case in pieces, the way a real call arrives. Your only job here is reasoning: decide which of the four perfusion requirements failed, and say how the vital signs and skin told you.

The case: a 19-year-old male roofer. Thirty minutes ago he fell about ten feet from a ladder and landed on his left side. He refused to stop working. His foreman found him sitting on the curb and called for help.

steps.prompt:
He is awake and answers every question correctly, but he keeps shifting position and asks you twice whether he is going to be okay. Skin is pale, cool and damp. Lung sounds are clear and equal. There is no visible bleeding.

From the first set of numbers alone, what is your leading impression?

choices.text: Perfusion is already inadequate and being compensated for; find the cause.
choices.feedback: Correct. A pulse of 124 with pale cool damp skin is a sympathetic surge, and the surge exists to defend a pressure that is under threat. The normal-looking systolic is the compensation working, not evidence of health.

choices.text: He is anxious after a fall; the vital signs reflect adrenaline from the scare.
choices.feedback: Tempting and wrong. Fright can raise pulse and respirations, but it does not usually clamp the skin this hard or narrow the pulse pressure. Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion here, and you have not excluded anything yet.

choices.text: He is stable because his blood pressure and oxygen saturation are both normal.
choices.feedback: This is the classic error. Blood pressure is the last value to move, and an SpO2 of 98 percent only tells you the blood is loaded with oxygen, not that it is reaching tissue.

steps.prompt:
Work the numbers. His blood pressure is `118/96`.

What does that pairing specifically tell you?

choices.text: The pulse pressure is 22 mmHg, well below the normal 30 to 40, meaning arterioles are clamped.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Diastolic pressure largely reflects arteriolar resistance, so a diastolic driven up toward the systolic is vasoconstriction you can read off the cuff. A narrowing pulse pressure often shows before the systolic moves at all.

choices.text: The systolic of 118 is normal, so the reading is reassuring.
choices.feedback: Reading only the top number throws away half the information. The systolic here is being propped up precisely by the rise in the bottom number, which is the finding that should worry you.

choices.text: The diastolic of 96 suggests he has undiagnosed hypertension.
choices.feedback: Possible in a 60-year-old, unlikely in a 19-year-old thirty minutes after a fall, with pale cool skin and a pulse of 124. When several findings point one way, do not build a story around the one that fits worst.

steps.prompt:
Now rule the families in and out. Recall the four requirements for perfusion: pump, pipes, fluid, air.

Which requirement is most likely failing here?

choices.text: Fluid. Air is intact with clear lungs and SpO2 98; the pipes are clamped, not dilated; and a 19-year-old pump failing this fast has no supporting findings.
choices.feedback: That is the reasoning. Clear lungs and a good saturation take air off the table. Pale cool clamped skin is the opposite of distributive shock, which runs warm and dilated. No crackles, no distended neck veins, and no cardiac history argue against pump and obstruction. Volume loss is what is left, and the mechanism supplies a site.

choices.text: Pipes. The skin findings point to vasodilation.
choices.feedback: The skin findings point the other way. Distributive shock gives warm, flushed, dry skin early because vessels are open. Pale, cool and damp means vessels are squeezed shut, which is compensation for something else.

choices.text: Air. The respiratory rate of 24 shows a breathing problem.
choices.feedback: The tachypnea is real, but with clear lungs and an SpO2 of 98 percent the lungs are doing their job. That rate is helping clear the lactic acid building in underperfused tissue, which is compensation, not the primary failure.

steps.prompt:
He landed on his left side. On exam, the left lower ribs are tender and there is a spreading bruise over the left flank. He winces when you palpate the left upper abdomen.

What does this add?

choices.text: A plausible internal bleeding site: the spleen sits under the left lower ribs.
choices.feedback: Right. The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt left-sided trauma, and it can bleed steadily into the abdomen with nothing visible from the outside. The absence of external blood never rules out hemorrhage.

choices.text: Rib pain explaining the fast breathing, so no further concern.
choices.feedback: Rib pain does cause shallow, rapid breathing, so that part is reasonable. But it explains only one finding and leaves the tachycardia, skin and narrow pulse pressure unaccounted for.

choices.text: Bruising means bleeding has already stopped in the skin, so the picture should improve.
choices.feedback: Surface bruising says nothing about what is happening underneath. A visible bruise over the flank after this mechanism raises concern for deeper injury rather than settling it.

steps.prompt:
Ten minutes later you repeat the vitals. He now answers slowly and asks the same question twice.

What has changed, and what does it mean?

choices.text: Compensation is failing: pulse up, systolic falling, mental status slipping. This is decompensated hypovolemic shock.
choices.feedback: Correct. The systolic dropping while the pulse climbs means rate and vessel tone can no longer hold the line. The mental status change is the brain reporting its own perfusion, and it is the most sensitive organ you have.

choices.text: He is improving, since the blood pressure came down toward a healthier number.
choices.feedback: A falling pressure in a bleeding patient is never improvement. Read it alongside the rising pulse and falling GCS, and the direction of the whole picture is unmistakable.

choices.text: The SpO2 is still 97 percent, so oxygenation is fine and nothing urgent has changed.
choices.feedback: Oxygenation is fine, which is exactly the trap. Pulse oximetry measures how loaded the blood is, not whether enough of it is arriving. You can have a saturation of 97 percent while bleeding to death.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: **tachycardia plus clamped skin plus a narrowing pulse pressure is shock, and a normal systolic is part of the picture, not an argument against it.**

Run the four requirements every time. Air was intact (clear lungs, SpO2 98). Pipes were clamped rather than dilated, which rules out distributive shock and points at compensation. The pump had no backup findings, no crackles and no distended neck veins, which rules out cardiogenic and obstructive. Fluid is what remains, and the mechanism named the organ.

The second set of vitals is the lesson in one frame: pulse 124 to 138, systolic 118 to 94, GCS 15 to 14. Compensation bought about forty minutes of normal-looking numbers, and when it ran out it ran out quickly. A single set of vitals gives you a snapshot; two sets separated by ten minutes give you a direction, and direction is what decides the plan.
